opus-5.5.text:
I think it's less useful than people often assume. I get asked for my "p(doom)" a lot, and I understand why. It's a compact way to signal how seriously you take the problem. But I don't think the number itself does much work.

For one thing, the estimates are extremely uncertain. If I said 10% or 30%, what's the error bar on that? It's huge, and the number depends a lot on how you carve up the scenarios. What counts as "very bad"? Over what time frame? Conditional on what kinds of policy responses? People often end up arguing past each other because they're answering slightly different questions.

More importantly, I don't think it changes what I should do day to day. Whether the probability is 5% or 50%, it's clearly high enough that we should be working really hard on alignment. The decision-relevant questions are more concrete. Which research directions are most promising? Where are the biggest gaps? What would we need to see to be confident a given system is safe to deploy? Those are the things I'd rather spend time on.

There's also a framing issue I care about. A single probability can make the outcome sound like something fixed, like a weather forecast we're just observing. But it isn't. It depends heavily on choices people make: how much effort goes into alignment, how carefully labs deploy, whether we build good evaluation methods. I'd rather think of it as a problem we can make progress on than a number we're trying to predict.

So I'm not against people doing the exercise. It can be useful for checking your own consistency, or for noticing when your views have shifted. But I'd put much more emphasis on the concrete technical and governance work that actually moves the outcome.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's useful, but mostly as a communication device rather than as a precise claim. When I say something like "I think there's a 10 to 90 percent chance things go badly" — and honestly, my own range is that wide — what I'm really communicating is that this is a serious possibility, serious enough that we should be putting a lot of effort into reducing it, and that I don't think anyone has a tight model of how this plays out.

The thing I'd push back on is treating the number itself as the important output. If someone tells me they're at 5 percent and someone else says 50 percent, the interesting conversation isn't about who's right — it's about what's driving the disagreement. Do they disagree about how hard alignment is technically? About whether labs will actually be careful? About how fast capabilities improve? Those are things you can make progress on. The number is just a summary statistic of all those underlying beliefs, and the summary loses a lot of the information.

The other thing I'd say is that the probability isn't fixed — it's a function of what we do. That's actually the most important point for me. If the number were 90 percent no matter what, then the right response would be very different than if it's 90 percent by default but 10 percent if we do the work. I think we're much more in the second world. Alignment is a hard technical problem, but it's a problem we can make real progress on, and we've seen that — things like RLHF, scalable oversight, interpretability work, these are all moving the needle. So I'd rather spend my time on the "how do we drive the number down" question than on the "what exactly is the number" question.

Where I do find probabilities genuinely useful is in forcing people to be concrete. If you say "I'm worried about AI" that's compatible with almost anything. If you say "I think there's a 20 percent chance of catastrophe this century," you've committed to something, and now someone can ask why, and you have to actually lay out your reasoning. That discipline is valuable, even if the number at the end is pretty soft.

astra-6.text:
I think it can be useful, but I’m wary of putting too much weight on a single number. It forces you to be explicit about how seriously you take the risk, and it can help you make decisions. But there’s so much uncertainty here that a precise probability can suggest more knowledge than we actually have.

I’d be more interested in what’s behind the number. What are the scenarios you’re worried about? What would have to happen for those scenarios to play out? And what evidence would change your mind? Two people can give very different probabilities but still agree on a lot of the work we should be doing to make AI safer.

So I’d treat it as a starting point for a discussion, rather than the thing we ultimately need to settle.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it can be useful, but I’m wary of putting too much weight on a particular number. There’s so much uncertainty here, and people can mean quite different things by a very bad outcome, or be considering different timelines and assumptions about what we do in response.

The useful part is often asking why you believe the probability is high or low. What would have to go wrong? What evidence would change your mind? And which things could we do now that would make those outcomes less likely?

So I’d treat a probability as a way to make your beliefs more explicit and start that conversation, rather than as a precise measurement. For deciding whether to work on the problem, you might not need much precision: even a relatively small chance of a sufficiently bad outcome can warrant a serious effort to prevent it.
